clue.text: Glistened and nearly boiled, keeping hot

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: to simmer is to cook just below boiling point
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A pan of water on the stove shimmers as it heats up, almost at the boil.
explanation.walkthrough: Simmering is cooking just short of a full boil, which is why 'nearly boiled' fits; the hot letter slips in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To shimmer is to shine with a soft wavering light, a close synonym of glisten.

clue.text: Most challenging mountain son conquers?

indicators.note: a climber who conquers a peak stands on its top, so in a down entry the son is placed above

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
the world's highest mountain

explanation.surface: A son climbs the toughest peak of all and conquers it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer the son sits on top of the mountain, as a climber who has conquered it would; the question mark flags that playful image.
explanation.definitionFit: Severest is the superlative of severe, meaning most demanding, harsh or difficult to cope with.

clue.text: In the wrong order, were allowed to enter pricy bar

indicators.note: the two words of the phrase must be swapped round from their natural sequence

blocks.note: to enter is to go in
with enter, the phrase means got in

explanation.surface: Someone describes a muddled evening: they were let into an expensive bar, but the events came out jumbled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Were allowed to enter' is the phrase got in; the opening words tell you to say its two halves the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingot is a block of cast metal, often gold, so a costly bar in a literal sense.

clue.text: Nuts, margarine, and no fruit

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters that follow have gone mad and are scrambled

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A shopping list reading nuts, margarine and no fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like the first item on a list, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandarin orange is a small loose-skinned citrus, a type of fruit.

clue.text: Filthier than anyone?

blocks.note: surface reading: the dirtiest person of all
setter's reading: from the phrase filthy rich, meaning extremely wealthy

explanation.walkthrough: Filthy rich means hugely wealthy, so the one who is most 'filthy' in that sense has the most money.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of a word for wealthy names the person with more money than everyone else.

clue.text: Relaxation in wigwam with river all around

indicators.note: something all around another encloses it on every side

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland, and another in Wales and England
a wigwam is a kind of tent

explanation.surface: Someone unwinds in a wigwam beside a river that surrounds it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a favourite crossword river; a wigwam is a cone-shaped tent of the North American plains.
explanation.definitionFit: Détente is an easing of tension between rival states, a political relaxation of hostility.

clue.text: Swindle captured by one’s camera

indicators.note: the answer is caught inside the words that follow, like a picture held by a camera

blocks.note: running across the end of one's and the start of camera

explanation.surface: A con trick caught on someone's camera.
explanation.definitionFit: A scam is a dishonest scheme to cheat people out of money, the same as a swindle.

clue.text: One meticulous in temporary role?

definitions.note: adjectival, as in a caretaker government

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: someone who takes care
second meaning: holding a post only until a permanent appointment is made

explanation.surface: A stand-in who is very careful while covering the job for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as care-taker for the first sense; the question mark admits that reading is playful.
explanation.definitionFit: A caretaker manager or government holds office for an interim period; a care-taker literally takes pains.

clue.text: SE Asian cradles daughter in illness

indicators.note: to cradle is to hold something closely inside your arms

blocks.note: a Malay is a person from Malaysia or the surrounding region
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A Southeast Asian mother cradles her sick daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: MALAY holds D: MALA(D)Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A malady is a disease or ailment, a slightly formal synonym of sickness.

clue.text: Retiree perhaps finds rotten pear nauseating

indicators.note: something rotten has broken down and decayed, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An older person complains that a rotten pear makes them feel sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten' reads as describing the pear, but it is the signal to rearrange both words.
explanation.definitionFit: A septuagenarian is someone in their seventies, an age at which many have stopped work, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: A whole kingdom’s products I refuse to touch

definitions.text: A whole kingdom’s products I refuse to touch

blocks.clueFragment: A whole kingdom’s products I refuse to touch
blocks.note: surface reading: someone boycotting everything a particular country makes
setter's reading: the animal kingdom, whose products are meat, milk, eggs, honey and leather

explanation.walkthrough: 'Kingdom' suggests a nation; in biology the animal kingdom is a kingdom, and shunning all its products describes a strict diet and lifestyle.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who eats and uses nothing derived from animals avoids meat, dairy, eggs and leather entirely.

clue.text: Halted car, travelling to church

indicators.note: travelling means moving about, so the letters are moved into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A car stops while on its way to a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Halted' and 'travelling' contradict each other in the picture, a hint that 'travelling' is doing a different job.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral is the principal church of a diocese, seat of a bishop.

clue.text: Competitive struggle to catch up the Pied Piper?

definitions.text: to catch up the Pied Piper?
definitions.note: a cryptic description, read as a race of rats

blocks.note: first meaning: the relentless scramble for success at work

blocks.clueFragment: to catch up the Pied Piper?
blocks.note: second meaning, playful: the rats of Hamelin racing after the piper who lured them away

explanation.walkthrough: In the legend the Pied Piper of Hamelin played his pipe and every rat in town followed him; the question mark admits the race is a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes the exhausting competitive grind of modern working life, a well-known idiom.

clue.text: Wrote in symbols ‘This is no bear’

blocks.note: 'no' here stands for 'not a', as in 'this is no ordinary day'
ted is short for teddy, a toy bear

explanation.surface: A caption written in musical or code symbols declaring that something is not a bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This is no bear' becomes 'this is not a ted'; the quotation marks frame it as a phrase to be rewritten.
explanation.definitionFit: Notated means set down in a system of notation, such as written music, using signs instead of words.

clue.text: One behind betrayal?

blocks.note: 'one' as in 'land one on him': a blow or thrust
at the rear, read as a place on the body

explanation.surface: Asking who was responsible for a treacherous act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One behind' reads as the person behind the betrayal; instead it is a blow landed from behind.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a treacherous act against someone who trusted you, a disloyal attack.

clue.text: Receptive sailor dispatched round the world?

indicators.note: to be sent round something is to go about it, enclosing it on all sides

blocks.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a common sailor
to dispatch is to send off
an orb is a sphere, a figure for the globe

explanation.surface: A sailor sent off on a voyage around the globe is open to new experiences.
explanation.walkthrough: AB stands for able-bodied seaman, the crossword's usual sailor; the round globe is the orb sitting inside the dispatching word.
explanation.definitionFit: Absorbent means able to soak things up, so readily taking in ideas or fluids.

clue.text: Quiet and strongly built, indicated resignation

blocks.note: sh is the instruction to be quiet
rugged describes a sturdy, robust build

explanation.surface: A silent, burly man showed that he was giving up.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting and dropping the shoulders is a gesture of indifference or helpless acceptance of something.

clue.text: Cops shan’t dare to abuse this power?

indicators.note: abusing something means misusing it and mangling it, so the letters are mistreated into a new order

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A warning that police officers must not misuse a particular authority they hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also works as a comment on the power, which critics say officers have abused; in Britain it lets police stop and search people in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a police power in the UK to halt a person and check them for weapons or drugs.

clue.text: Bust I leer at in studio

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters are smashed and reassembled

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An art student confesses to ogling a sculpted bust in the studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a sculpture or a body part to leer at, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is an artist's or designer's workshop, borrowed from French.

clue.text: Graciously agrees to accept small sketches

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: to deign is to condescend graciously to do something
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Someone kindly consents to take a few little drawings.
explanation.walkthrough: DEIGNS takes in S: DE(S)IGNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Designs are drawings or plans made to show how something will look, so preparatory sketches.

clue.text: Was impatient to be given meal after tea

indicators.note: after places one piece following the other in the answer

blocks.note: cha is a British slang word for tea
to be fed is to be given food

explanation.surface: Someone grew restless waiting for dinner after afternoon tea.
explanation.definitionFit: To chafe is to feel irritated or restless at some restriction or delay.

clue.text: Holding container, present greenstuff

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: present in the sense of being here, not away
a bag is a container

explanation.surface: A gift box with leafy greens inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift, but it means here, in attendance. HERE holds BAG: HER(BAG)E.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbage is grass and leafy plants collectively, especially as grazing for animals.

clue.text: Ballet group in Berlin prison

definitions.note: the first word of the band name Spandau Ballet

blocks.note: first meaning: read with Ballet as the band ... Ballet, a 1980s British pop group
second meaning: the jail in the west of Berlin that held Nazi war criminals such as Rudolf Hess

explanation.surface: A dance company performing inside a Berlin jail.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests dancers; 'Ballet group' instead points to the 1980s pop band named after the Berlin district, so the answer is the word that goes with Ballet.
explanation.definitionFit: The district of Berlin gave its name both to the war-criminals' prison and to the British new-romantic band.

clue.text: Move aimlessly; meaning?

blocks.note: first meaning: to wander or float without purpose
second meaning: the general sense, as in 'get my ...'

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites you to read 'meaning?' as asking what the first phrase means; it is a second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for being carried along without direction and a noun for the gist of what someone says.

clue.text: Young bird made escape, landing finally by heather

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word it follows, keeping only its closing letter

blocks.note: to flee is to make one's escape
the last letter of landing
ling is another name for common heather

explanation.surface: A young bird escapes the nest and comes down in the heather.
explanation.definitionFit: A fledgling is a chick that has just grown its feathers and is learning to fly.

clue.text: As for cake, it is said to be welcome but not essential

definitions.text: As for cake, it is said to be welcome but not essential

blocks.clueFragment: As for cake, it is said to be welcome but not essential
blocks.note: surface reading: a general remark that cake is a pleasant treat but hardly a necessity
setter's reading: the idiom about the topping on a cake, meaning an extra pleasure on top of something already good

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'the ... on the cake' describes a nice extra that is not needed; on an actual cake, the sweet coating is the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The sugary coating on a cake is a pleasant addition rather than a necessary part, as the idiom says.

clue.text: On and off I’d lost, as …

indicators.note: on and off means intermittently, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of these words

explanation.surface: Someone trailing off mid-sentence, admitting they had intermittently lost track.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the ellipsis itself: the printed three dots at the end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An ellipsis is printed as a row of three small points, so the symbol at the end of the clue is literally those marks.

clue.text: One’s tread wildly echoed

indicators.note: wildly means in an uncontrolled way, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone's heavy footsteps rang out loudly through an empty hall.
explanation.definitionFit: To resonate is to produce a deep, reverberating sound, the same as ringing back as an echo does.
